issues.subcategory: erroneous significance claim
issues.description: The Discussion explicitly states that the meta-analytic effect size for 'Opportunity to Connect with Others' was 'significantly different from zero.' However, the Results section clearly reports p = .065 for this outcome, which is not statistically significant at any conventional alpha level. The 95% CI [-.01, .18] also barely includes zero, confirming non-significance. This is a direct factual error that misrepresents the primary statistical outcome for this outcome variable and will mislead readers.
issues.quote: the meta-analytic effect size was .09, and significantly different from zero

issues.subcategory: internal numerical inconsistency in fail-safe N
issues.description: The Fail-Safe N (FSN) values reported in the Results section differ from those cited in the Discussion for two of the four outcome variables. For 'Opportunity to Express Self,' Results report FSN = 3, but the Discussion states 'only five unreported studies.' For 'Opportunity to Connect with Others,' Results report FSN = 5, but the Discussion refers to 'the low FSN (11 studies).' These are not rounding differences—they are categorically different numbers. Such inconsistencies undermine trust in the accuracy of all numerical reporting throughout the paper.
issues.quote: The FSN was 3 studies. [Results, Express] ... only five unreported studies could reduce the results [Discussion, Express] ... The FSN was 5 studies. [Results, Connect] ... the low FSN (11 studies) [Discussion, Connect]

issues.subcategory: confidence interval reported as prediction interval
issues.description: In the Discussion of 'Self-Disclosure Safety,' the authors write 'The 95% PI [-.40, -.15] indicated that future studies would be likely to find such an effect.' However, the Results section reports the 95% CI as [-.40, -.15] and the 95% PI as [-.54, -.03] for this same outcome. The CI and PI are therefore swapped in the Discussion. The CI reflects precision of the mean estimate; the PI indicates where 95% of true individual study effects are expected to fall. Substituting the narrower CI for the PI makes the effect appear far more stable across future studies than the actual PI supports.
issues.quote: The 95% PI [-.40, -.15] indicated that future studies would be likely to find such an effect as well.

issues.subcategory: abstract contradicts results section
issues.description: The abstract states that for self-expression 'all 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for effect sizes included zero,' implying a uniformly null finding. However, the Results section reports that the summary meta-analytic 95% CI was [.01, .14], which explicitly and entirely excludes zero (p = .021). The abstract's claim is therefore factually incorrect. This directly contradicts the authors' own reported statistics and will mislead any reader who relies on the abstract alone, which is a very large proportion of scientific consumers.
issues.quote: self-esteem did not relate to perceived opportunities for self-expression (across the seven replications, all 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for effect sizes included zero)

issues.subcategory: stated minimum sample size not met
issues.description: The Methods section states that all studies 'collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP (120 for the present study to ensure adequate statistical power).' However, five of the seven included studies fall below this stated minimum: BYU-Sp16 (N=90), BYU-Wi17 (N=90), Gordon (N=80), IIT-Sp17 (N=94), and SAU (N=81). The paper simultaneously claims all studies met the requirement and then reports sample sizes that contradict this claim. This is either a factual misstatement or means studies that violated a preregistered protocol requirement were included without justification or sensitivity analysis.
issues.quote: All studies in this meta-analysis received this approval by the CREP team, collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP (120 for the present study to ensure adequate statistical power)

issues.subcategory: original effect size inconsistency across sections
issues.description: The original effect size for 'Self-Disclosure Advantages' is reported as -.30 in the abstract and as β = -.300 in Table 1, but is reported as r = -.33 in Table 3 and as '-.33' in the Discussion. In simple bivariate regression with standardized variables (as used here), β and r are algebraically identical, so they must be equal. The discrepancy cannot be attributed to rounding. This unexplained inconsistency suggests a computation or transcription error in one of the locations and affects all comparisons involving this key original benchmark value.
issues.quote: meta analytic effect size = -.16, original effect size = -.30 [abstract] ... Original | Forest & Wood | ... | -.300 | .011 [Table 1] ... BYU-Sp16 | -0.02 | -0.33 [Table 3] ... vs. -.33 [discussion]

issues.subcategory: selective dismissal of a significant meta-analytic result
issues.description: The meta-analytic result for 'Opportunity to Express Self' is statistically significant (r = .08, p = .021, 95% CI [.01, .14]), yet the authors conclude there is no effect for this outcome. They justify this by noting that individual replications are non-significant. This reasoning is internally inconsistent: the entire purpose of meta-analysis is to aggregate studies to achieve power beyond that of any single study. Declaring a significant meta-analytic result null because constituent studies are individually non-significant inverts the logic of aggregation. The positive direction of the meta-analytic result (+.08) also differs from the expected negative direction and deserves acknowledgment.
issues.quote: Even though the effect size meta-analysis revealed that the point-estimate meta-analytic effect size of the seven replication studies, r = .08, p = .021, was statistically different from zero...all individual replications found regression coefficients not significantly different from zero.

issues.subcategory: prediction interval values inconsistent between sections
issues.description: For the 'Opportunity to Connect with Others' outcome, the Results section reports the 95% PI as [-.09, .26], but the Discussion reports a 95% PI of [-.07, .27] for the same outcome. These values differ numerically and cannot both be correct. Since the PI is a central piece of evidence in the authors' argument about expected future effects, this inconsistency materially affects how readers should interpret the stability of the connection finding.
issues.quote: 95% PI [-.09, .26] [Results section] ... supported by the 95% PI of [-.07, .27] [Discussion section]

issues.subcategory: uncontrolled methodological heterogeneity across sites
issues.description: Seven studies vary on multiple procedural dimensions simultaneously: (1) RSE response scale (4-point in 5 studies vs. 5-point in 2 studies); (2) data collection mode (in-lab only, online only, or mixed); (3) individual vs. group administration (SAU ran groups of 2–6); (4) RSE item wording differences in IIT-Sp16 (4 of 10 items altered); and (5) composite scoring method (Gordon likely summed items; others averaged). Each of these variations can independently shift effect size estimates. Despite this, the authors treat all studies as methodologically equivalent in the meta-analysis and explicitly decline to examine moderators, leaving unexplained variance attributable to procedural artifacts.
issues.quote: researchers employed both methods (three replications had participants complete in lab only, two used online only, and two used both methods)...the SAU replication, which ran participants in groups of two to six. Two other known differences across replications involved minor discrepancies in presentation of the RSE scale

issues.subcategory: composite scoring inconsistency affecting comparability
issues.description: The paper states that items were mean-averaged across studies, but acknowledges that 'the Gordon study's mean implied items were summed.' Summing rather than averaging produces scores on a qualitatively different scale (e.g., a 9-item subscale summed over 1–7 ranges from 9 to 63 rather than 1 to 7). Regression coefficients from the Gordon study are therefore not directly comparable to those from the other six studies. Inclusion of the Gordon study without correction or exclusion sensitivity analysis potentially distorts the meta-analytic estimates.
issues.quote: the Gordon study's mean implied items were summed.

issues.subcategory: meta-analysis protocol not preregistered
issues.description: The paper prominently claims preregistration as a methodological strength. However, only the individual replication studies were preregistered. The meta-analytic protocol—including study inclusion criteria, analytic model selection, choice of heterogeneity estimator, and outcomes to synthesize—was not preregistered. This distinction is important: decisions made after seeing data (e.g., selecting REML over DL based on 'interpretability') constitute researcher degrees of freedom in the meta-analysis itself. A preregistered meta-analytic protocol would have been needed for the replication badge to extend to the synthesis.
issues.quote: This manuscript qualifies for a Preregistration badge; the data collection and data analysis methods were preregistered at each individual study's OSF page

issues.subcategory: potential attrition bias from excluded replication attempts
issues.description: The paper notes that 17 forks (potential replication teams) were started on the CREP OSF page but only 7 contributed usable data. The fate of the other 10 teams is entirely undisclosed. If any of those teams collected data but failed to post results because of null or contrary findings, their exclusion constitutes a form of small-study publication bias within the project itself—the very problem CREP was designed to address. The inclusion criterion ('posted data and results') could systematically exclude failed or null replications.
issues.quote: The Forest and Wood (2012) CREP replication project page on the OSF has 17 'forks' representing research teams or institutions that have started the replication process...These teams generated seven studies that met the minimum sample size, and posted data and results

issues.subcategory: post-hoc meta-analytic model selection
issues.description: The authors report comparing REML and DL estimators and selecting REML 'as it produced more interpretable heterogeneity estimates.' 'More interpretable' is a subjective and circular criterion—it could mean 'estimates more consistent with our preferred interpretation.' Model selection should be based on pre-specified statistical rationale (e.g., simulation evidence for small-k meta-analyses, expected heterogeneity structure) rather than on the outputs the model produces. This post-hoc selection introduces researcher degrees of freedom into the meta-analytic results.
issues.quote: We compared restricted maximum likelihood (REML) and DerSimonian and Laird (DL) models and selected REML as it produced more interpretable heterogeneity estimates for our data

issues.subcategory: inadequate and outdated publication bias assessment
issues.description: Publication bias is assessed solely via Rosenthal's fail-safe N (FSN), a method widely criticized in current meta-science for producing misleadingly large values, ignoring effect size distributions, and not accounting for small-study effects. Modern methods such as Egger's regression, trim-and-fill, PET-PEESE, p-curve, or p-uniform are substantially more informative and should be reported instead of, or alongside, the FSN. While the small k (7 studies) limits power for these tests, their application and limitations should be explicitly addressed rather than relying exclusively on a deprecated approach.
issues.quote: we conducted a fail-safe number (FSN) analysis (Rosenberg, 2005) using the fsn function. The FSN analysis was intended to identify the number of non-significant, unreported studies required to add to the meta-analysis to reduce a significant meta-analytic result to non-significance.

issues.subcategory: multiple comparisons without correction
issues.description: Four dependent variables are simultaneously tested using regression across seven studies (28 individual tests), plus four meta-analytic tests. No correction for multiple comparisons is applied or even discussed. The family-wise error rate across these tests is substantially inflated above the nominal alpha. For example, at α = .05, the probability of at least one false positive across 28 independent tests exceeds 75%. The authors' selective interpretation of which results 'replicated' is therefore potentially driven by chance positive findings.
issues.quote: For each of the four outcome variables, we present the standardized beta and p-value for the regressions.

issues.subcategory: heterogeneity statistics unreliable but reported as substantive
issues.description: The authors acknowledge in the Limitations section that 'heterogeneity measures are known to be biased for meta-analysis involving small numbers of studies,' citing von Hippel (2015). However, the Results section presents specific I² values (e.g., I² = 71.76%, 95% CI [27.06%, 94.69%] for safety; I² = 44.39% for connect) as meaningful indicators of between-study variance and uses them to characterize findings. Reporting statistics as substantive while simultaneously acknowledging they are unreliable is methodologically inconsistent and gives readers unwarranted confidence in the heterogeneity estimates.
issues.quote: The between-study variance showed some evidence of heterogeniety, Q(df = 6) = 18.69, p = 0.005; T2 = .02, 95% CI [0, .15]; I2 = 71.76%, 95% CI [27.06%, 94.69%]

issues.subcategory: prediction interval misinterpreted
issues.description: Prediction intervals are repeatedly interpreted as indicating 'what 95% of future studies would find,' for example: 'the 95% CI and prediction interval (PI) indicated future studies would show an effect size between .01 and .14.' A PI does not mean that 95% of future sample estimates will fall within the interval—it represents the expected range of true population effects given estimated mean and heterogeneity. Actual future study estimates also depend on sampling error proportional to each study's N. This misinterpretation systematically overstates the precision of the prediction and conflates the distribution of true effects with the distribution of observed estimates.
issues.quote: the 95% CI and prediction interval (PI) indicated future studies would show an effect size between .01 and .14 (smaller than the original)

issues.subcategory: fail-safe N logic inverted
issues.description: The Discussion uses the small FSN for the expression outcome to argue confidence in a null effect: 'The FSN analysis, which indicated that only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant, led us to be confident that future replications would find the same lack of an effect.' This reasoning inverts the FSN logic. A small FSN means a significant result (here, p = .021) is fragile and easily overturned—it should increase skepticism about the significant result, not confirm the null. The conclusion drawn from the FSN is the opposite of what the statistic implies.
issues.quote: The FSN analysis, which indicated that only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant, led us to be confident that future replications would find the same lack of an effect as our replications.

issues.subcategory: oversimplified p-value distribution claim
issues.description: The authors argue that because the original connect result had p = .05, and 'p-values between .04 and .05 have been demonstrated to be relatively more likely in the case of a true null hypothesis than a false one,' this constitutes evidence against the original finding. The Masicampo & Lalande (2012) observation is a population-level finding about the distribution of p-values across many published studies, consistent with p-hacking, and does not logically imply that any single p ≈ .05 result is more likely to be a false positive. Applying a distributional population-level statistic to make inferences about a single observed p-value is a base-rate fallacy.
issues.quote: it is worth noting that the original study obtained a p-value of .05, and p-values between .04 and .05 have been demonstrated to be relatively more likely in the case of a true null hypothesis than a false one

issues.subcategory: independence assumption violated in SAU replication
issues.description: The SAU replication administered questionnaires to groups of 2–6 participants simultaneously in the same space. Social survey responses completed in the presence of others are not statistically independent—participants may observe each other's reactions, experience demand characteristics from group norms, or otherwise influence one another's responses. This violates a core assumption of the regression analyses used (and of the meta-analysis that treats this study as independent from others). The effect this has on the SAU effect size estimates is unknown but could bias them in either direction.
issues.quote: Participants completing questionnaires in the lab did so alone, except for the SAU replication, which ran participants in groups of two to six.

issues.subcategory: RSE scale and item modifications compromise measurement equivalence
issues.description: Two studies (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) used a 5-point RSE response scale instead of the standard 4-point scale, altering the variance and distribution of scores. IIT-Sp16 additionally altered the wording of 4 of 10 RSE items (e.g., 'At times I think I am no good at all' vs. 'I think I am no good at all'), potentially changing item difficulty and factor loadings. Neither modification is justified or tested for equivalence to the standard scale. Combining standardized regression coefficients from studies using non-equivalent measurements of the same construct introduces construct validity problems that are not adequately acknowledged.
issues.quote: most replications used the original four-point scale, while two replications (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) used a five-point scale...one study (IIT-Sp16) had slight differences in item order and in wording on four out of ten items (e.g., 'At times I think I am no good at all' vs. 'I think I am no good at all')

issues.subcategory: causal language applied to cross-sectional correlational data
issues.description: Throughout the manuscript, self-esteem is described as 'predicting' Facebook perceptions in language that implies directionality or causation. The study is entirely cross-sectional and correlational; no experimental manipulation is present. It is equally plausible that habitual positive Facebook interactions boost self-esteem, that a third variable (e.g., social anxiety, neuroticism) drives both, or that the direction reverses under different conditions. The theoretical framing of 'social compensation' further reinforces a causal story that the data cannot support.
issues.quote: self-esteem negatively predicted perceived safety of self-disclosure on Facebook as compared to face-to-face interactions...lower self-esteem was a significant predictor of perceiving Facebook as a safer place to self-disclose

issues.subcategory: unsubstantiated publication bias attribution
issues.description: The Discussion concludes that effect sizes smaller in the replications than in the original constitute evidence of 'publication bias in the original study.' However, smaller replication effects relative to originals are expected for multiple non-bias-related reasons: regression to the mean (winner's curse from selecting studies with large initial estimates), temporal changes in Facebook usage patterns between 2012 and 2016–2017, population differences across sites, and methodological variation. No formal test comparing the original to the replication distribution (e.g., excess significance test, p-curve) is conducted to attribute the decline specifically to publication bias.
issues.quote: all factors indicating the presence of publication bias in the original study

issues.subcategory: Facebook usage not assessed as covariate or inclusion criterion
issues.description: The study measures perceptions of Facebook specifically, yet Facebook usage frequency was not assessed and non-users were not excluded. By 2016–2017, a substantial proportion of college-aged participants had shifted primary social media use to Instagram and Snapchat. Participants who rarely or never use Facebook would provide meaningless or floor-level responses to Facebook perception items, attenuating true effect sizes and introducing measurement error. The authors acknowledge this temporal confound but do not address it as a potential inclusion criterion or covariate.
issues.quote: both Snapchat and Instagram were among a new crop of social media outlets for US and UK participants that challenged Facebook as the preferred social networking site for the age cohort of the participants in this research

issues.subcategory: CREP acronym given three different full names
issues.description: The acronym CREP is expanded to three different names across the manuscript: 'Collaborative Replication and Education Project' (abstract), 'Collaborative Research and Education Project' (introduction), and 'Collaborative Replications and Education Project' (reference list). Only one of these can be correct. This inconsistency suggests inadequate proofreading and may confuse readers attempting to locate the project.
issues.quote: Collaborative Replication and Education Project (CREP) [abstract] ... Collaborative Research and Education Project (CREP; Grahe, et al., 2016) [introduction] ... Collaborative Replications and Education Project (CREP) [reference]

issues.subcategory: Table 2 absent from manuscript
issues.description: The Results section states 'Table 2 shows each study's descriptive statistics for gender, race, and the mean and standard deviation for self-esteem and each of the four outcome variables.' However, Table 2 is not reproduced in the submitted manuscript. Readers cannot verify the descriptive statistics referenced in the text, and the note 'n/a = Data not available. n/c = Data not collected' appears without the table it annotates.
issues.quote: Table 2 shows each study's descriptive statistics for gender, race, and the mean and standard deviation for self-esteem and each of the four outcome variables.

issues.subcategory: reference author name misspelled in text citation
issues.description: The author name 'Lalande' is spelled 'Lelande' in one in-text citation ('Masicampo & Lelande, 2012') but is correctly spelled 'Lalande' in the reference list. Additionally, 'Pashler' is spelled 'Paschler' in one in-text citation. These are factual errors that would impede verification or retrieval.
issues.quote: Masicampo & Lelande, 2012

issues.subcategory: Table 1 duplicate author column
issues.description: The structure of Table 1 contains a duplicated 'Authors' column header, producing a redundant column in the table. This is a formatting error that reduces readability and suggests incomplete quality control during manuscript preparation.
issues.quote: Study | Authors | Authors | N | β | p

issues.subcategory: misspelling of 'publicly' and 'heterogeneity'
issues.description: 'Publicly' is consistently spelled 'publically' throughout the manuscript, and 'heterogeneity' is consistently spelled 'heterogeniety' in multiple locations. These are recurring errors that detract from the manuscript's professional presentation.
issues.quote: Data and results are made publically available on the Open Science Framework ... heterogeniety of the host institution population

issues.subcategory: missing data handling undocumented and inconsistent
issues.description: The authors acknowledge that 'not all studies posted analysis scripts or narratives to help us determine such things as missing data handling, composite score calculations, data exclusions, etc.' Different approaches to missing data (listwise deletion, pairwise deletion, or imputation) can produce different sample sizes, different variance estimates, and systematically different effect sizes. Without knowing how each study handled missing data, the comparability of effect sizes across studies is uncertain, and the source of any observed heterogeneity is uninterpretable.
issues.quote: not all studies posted analysis scripts or narratives to help us determine such things as missing data handling, composite score calculations, data exclusions, etc.
